fields.meta_title: What Is Spiritual Warfare? A Biblical Guide
fields.description: The Christian life is a battlefield against unseen spiritual forces — but the enemy is already defeated. Here is what spiritual warfare is and how to stand firm.
fields.body_html:
The Christian life is not a playground but a battlefield. From the moment we belong to Christ, we are caught up in a real conflict — not against other people, but against unseen spiritual forces of evil that oppose God and seek to destroy his work in us and through us. This is what the Bible calls spiritual warfare. It can be a subject of both unhealthy obsession, which sees a demon behind every difficulty, and unhealthy neglect, which forgets the enemy exists. Scripture treats it soberly and hopefully: the enemy is real and dangerous, and yet already defeated, so that the believer fights not for victory but from a victory Christ has already won on the cross. “Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (Ephesians 6:10). Here is what spiritual warfare is, how the enemy works, and how a believer can stand firm and unafraid.

The battle is real — but not against people

Paul names the conflict plainly: “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6:12). This reframes how a Christian sees the world. Our real enemies are not the people who oppose or wound us — they are, at most, pawns — but the spiritual powers behind the world’s evil. This truth guards us from bitterness toward people and points us to the actual source of the trouble.

Peter warns us to take the threat seriously: “Be sober-minded; be watchful. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). The devil is real, personal, and hostile — a liar and “the father of lies” (John 8:44), a tempter, an accuser. To pretend otherwise is to be dangerously naïve. Yet Scripture never leaves us afraid, because it always sets the enemy’s power against the far greater power of God.

The enemy is already defeated

Here is the truth that transforms spiritual warfare from terror into confidence: the decisive battle has already been won. At the cross, Jesus “disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them” (Colossians 2:15). The devil is a defeated foe, on a leash, awaiting his final doom. He can still tempt, accuse, and harass, but he cannot ultimately win, and he has no power over a believer except what is yielded to him.

So the Christian fights from strength, not weakness. “He who is in you is greater than he who is in the world” (1 John 4:4). We are not two equal powers locked in an uncertain struggle; we belong to the victorious Christ, and “in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). The believer’s confidence rests not on their own strength but on the finished triumph of Jesus. This is why we can be watchful without being fearful: the outcome is not in doubt.

Resist the devil, and he will flee

Because the enemy is defeated, the Christian’s calling is to resist him — to stand firm and refuse his lies. “Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Note the order: first we submit to God, drawing near to him, and then, standing in his strength, we resist the enemy, who flees. Resistance is not achieved by shouting at the devil but by clinging to God and standing on his truth.

Peter gives the same command with a promise of solidarity: “Resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same kinds of suffering are being experienced by your brotherhood throughout the world” (1 Peter 5:9). We resist by faith — by believing God’s word above the enemy’s whispers, by refusing temptation, by standing our ground when pressed. Much of spiritual warfare is exactly this: not dramatic confrontation but the daily, faithful refusal to give in, holding fast to Christ when we are tempted to doubt, fear, or sin.

Put on the whole armor of God

God has not sent us into battle unarmed. Paul describes the equipment in detail: “Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil” (Ephesians 6:11). The armour is the truth of the gospel applied to every part of us — the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the readiness of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith “with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one,” the helmet of salvation, and “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:14–17).

Notice that the armour is largely defensive, and its whole purpose is to stand — to hold the ground Christ has won, not to seize new territory by our own force. And notice that every piece is really Christ and his gospel: his truth, his righteousness, his salvation, his word, received and lived by faith. To put on the armour is to clothe ourselves daily in the gospel, so that when the enemy attacks we are covered by what God has provided rather than exposed in our own strength.

The weapons are prayer, the Word, and truth

The Christian’s true weapons are not worldly. “For though we walk in the flesh, we are not waging war according to the flesh. For the weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh but have divine power to destroy strongholds... We destroy arguments and every lofty opinion raised against the knowledge of God, and take every thought captive to obey Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:3–5). Much of the battle is fought in the mind — against lies, false accusations, and thoughts that exalt themselves against God — and the weapon is the truth of God’s word wielded in faith.

And prayer is the great atmosphere of the whole conflict. Paul ends his description of the armour with it: “praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication” (Ephesians 6:18). The believer who prays, feeds on Scripture, and holds fast to the truth is a believer clothed and armed. The old writers on holiness understood that our sin is one of the enemy’s chief footholds, so that putting sin to death and standing against the devil are closely joined — a heart kept clean and close to God is a fortress the enemy finds hard to breach.

Know the enemy’s tactics

Since the devil is a schemer, it helps to recognize how he works. Scripture warns us not to be “outwitted by Satan; for we are not ignorant of his designs” (2 Corinthians 2:11). His chief weapon is deception, not force — he is a liar who twists God’s word, sows doubt about God’s goodness, and dresses evil up as good: “even Satan disguises himself as an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14). He tempts us toward sin, then accuses us for it; he whispers that God does not love us, that his commands are burdensome, that we are beyond forgiveness.

Jesus summarized the enemy’s whole aim: “The thief comes only to steal and kill and destroy” — and then his own: “I came that they may have life and have it abundantly” (John 10:10). Knowing this, the believer learns to test every thought against God’s word, to distrust the whispers of condemnation and doubt, and to run to Christ rather than away from him when accused. Most of the enemy’s power lies in lies believed; the moment his lie is exposed by the truth, its grip begins to break.

Standing firm to the end

Spiritual warfare, rightly understood, is not a call to fear or to sensational hunting after demons, but to sober watchfulness and steady faith. The Christian stands guarded by Christ’s victory, clothed in his armour, armed with his word and prayer, resisting the enemy’s lies and refusing to yield. It is a daily discipline more than a series of dramatic events — the ongoing work of holding fast to Christ against everything that would pull us from him.

And the end is certain. Those who belong to Christ overcome “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (Revelation 12:11) — by trusting in Jesus’ finished work and confessing him faithfully to the end. So do not be afraid, and do not be careless. Draw near to God, put on his armour, take up his word, give yourself to prayer, and stand. The lion roars, but he is chained; the victory is already Christ’s, and all who are in him share it. Fight from that victory, and you cannot finally lose. And lift your eyes to the end of the war: a day is coming when the enemy is cast down forever and every battle is over, when the people of God will rest in unbroken peace and the roaring lion will trouble them no more.
